title: Vectors in the Plane
lead: A vector is a quantity with both magnitude and direction, drawn as an arrow. This section combines vectors by scalar multiplication, addition and subtraction, writes them in component form and through unit vectors, and uses them to find resultant forces and velocities.
objectives: Describe a plane vector, using correct notation.
Perform basic vector operations (scalar multiplication, addition, subtraction).
Express a vector in component form.
Explain the formula for the magnitude of a vector.
Express a vector in terms of unit vectors.
Give two examples of vector quantities.
summary_html:
• Vectors are used to represent quantities that have both magnitude and direction.
  • We can add vectors by using the parallelogram method or the triangle method to find the sum. We can multiply a vector by a scalar to change its length or give it the opposite direction.
  • Subtraction of vectors is defined in terms of adding the negative of the vector.
  • A vector is written in component form as $\kvecv=\langle x,y\rangle .$
  • The magnitude of a vector is a scalar: $\| \kvecv\| =\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}.$
  • A unit vector $\kvecu $ has magnitude $1$ and can be found by dividing a vector by its magnitude: $\kvecu=\frac{1}{\| \kvecv\|}\kvecv.$ The standard unit vectors are $\kveci=\langle 1,0\rangle \;\text{and}\;\kvecj=\langle 0,1\rangle .$ A vector $\kvecv=\langle x,y\rangle$ can be expressed in terms of the standard unit vectors as $\kvecv=x\kveci+y\kvecj.$
  • Vectors are often used in physics and engineering to represent forces and velocities, among other quantities.

exercises.prompt: Prove the additive inverse property.

answer.solution: Let $\mathbf{u}=\langle x_{1},y_{1}\rangle.$ By the definition of scalar multiplication, $-\mathbf{u}=(-1)\mathbf{u}=\langle -x_{1},-y_{1}\rangle.$ Adding in components and applying the additive inverse property of real numbers, $\mathbf{u}+(-\mathbf{u})=\langle x_{1}+(-x_{1}),y_{1}+(-y_{1})\rangle=\langle 0,0\rangle=\mathbf{0}.$ □
answer.hint: Use the component form of the vectors.

For the following exercises, use the given vectors $\text{a}$ and $\text{b}.$

$\text{a}=2\text{i}+\text{j},$ $\text{b}=\text{i}+3\text{j}$

answer.solution: a. $\text{a}+\text{b}=3\text{i}+4\text{j},$ $\text{a}+\text{b}=\langle 3,4\rangle ;$ b. $\text{a}-\text{b}=\text{i}-2\text{j},$ $\text{a}-\text{b}=\langle 1,-2\rangle ;$ c. Consider the vector $\text{a}(t)=\langle \cos t,\sin t\rangle$ with components that depend on a real number $t.$ As the number $t$ varies, the components of $\text{a}(t)$ change as well, depending on the functions that define them.

a. Write the vectors $\text{a}(0)$ and $\text{a}(\pi )$ in component form.

b. Show that the magnitude $\| \text{a}(t)\|$ of vector $\text{a}(t)$ remains constant for any real number $t.$

c. As $t$ varies, show that the terminal point of vector $\text{a}(t)$ describes a circle centered at the origin of radius $1.$

answer.solution:
a. $\mathbf{a}(0)=\langle\cos 0,\sin 0\rangle=\langle 1,0\rangle$ and $\mathbf{a}(\pi)=\langle\cos\pi,\sin\pi\rangle=\langle -1,0\rangle.$

b. $\|\mathbf{a}(t)\|=\sqrt{\cos^{2}t+\sin^{2}t}=\sqrt{1}=1$ for every real number $t,$ by the Pythagorean identity.

c. In standard position the terminal point of $\mathbf{a}(t)$ is $(x,y)=(\cos t,\sin t),$ so $x^{2}+y^{2}=\cos^{2}t+\sin^{2}t=1:$ every terminal point lies on the circle of radius 1 centered at the origin, and as $t$ runs over $[0,2\pi)$ the point $(\cos t,\sin t)$ reaches every point of that circle.

exercises.prompt: Show that vectors $\text{a}(t)=\langle \cos t,\sin t\rangle$ and $\text{a}(x)=\langle x,\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\rangle$ are equivalent for $x=1$ and $t=2k\pi ,$ where $k$ is an integer.

answer.solution: For $x=1,$ $\mathbf{a}(1)=\langle 1,\sqrt{1-1^{2}}\rangle=\langle 1,0\rangle.$ For $t=2k\pi$ with $k$ an integer, $\cos 2k\pi=1$ and $\sin 2k\pi=0,$ so $\mathbf{a}(2k\pi)=\langle 1,0\rangle.$ The two vectors have the same components, so they have the same magnitude, 1, and the same direction, and they are equivalent.

exercises.prompt: Show that vectors $\text{a}(t)=\langle \cos t,\sin t\rangle$ and $\text{a}(x)=\langle x,\sqrt{1-x^{2}}\rangle$ are opposite for $x=1$ and $t=\pi +2k\pi ,$ where $k$ is an integer.

answer.solution: For $x=1,$ $\mathbf{a}(1)=\langle 1,0\rangle.$ For $t=\pi+2k\pi,$ $\cos t=-1$ and $\sin t=0,$ so $\mathbf{a}(\pi+2k\pi)=\langle -1,0\rangle=-\langle 1,0\rangle.$ One vector is $(-1)$ times the other: they have the same magnitude, 1, and opposite directions, so they are opposite.

Let $\text{a}=\langle a_{1},a_{2}\rangle ,$ $\text{b}=\langle b_{1},b_{2}\rangle ,$ and $\text{c}=\langle c_{1},c_{2}\rangle$ be three nonzero vectors. If $a_{1}b_{2}-a_{2}b_{1}\ne 0,$ then show there are two scalars, $\alpha$ and $β,$ such that $\text{c}=\alpha \text{a}+β\text{b}.$

answer.solution: Writing $\mathbf{c}=\alpha\mathbf{a}+\beta\mathbf{b}$ in components gives the system $\alpha a_{1}+\beta b_{1}=c_{1}$ and $\alpha a_{2}+\beta b_{2}=c_{2}.$ Multiplying the first equation by $b_{2},$ the second by $b_{1},$ and subtracting eliminates $\beta:$ $\alpha(a_{1}b_{2}-a_{2}b_{1})=c_{1}b_{2}-c_{2}b_{1}.$ Eliminating $\alpha$ the same way gives $\beta(a_{1}b_{2}-a_{2}b_{1})=a_{1}c_{2}-a_{2}c_{1}.$ Since $a_{1}b_{2}-a_{2}b_{1}\ne 0,$ we can divide: $\alpha=\frac{c_{1}b_{2}-c_{2}b_{1}}{a_{1}b_{2}-a_{2}b_{1}}$ and $\beta=\frac{a_{1}c_{2}-a_{2}c_{1}}{a_{1}b_{2}-a_{2}b_{1}},$ and these two scalars satisfy $\mathbf{c}=\alpha\mathbf{a}+\beta\mathbf{b}.$

exercises.prompt:
Let $P(x_{0},f(x_{0}))$ be a fixed point on the graph of the differentiable function $f$ with a domain that is the set of real numbers.

a. Determine the real number $z_{0}$ such that point $Q(x_{0}+1,z_{0})$ is situated on the line tangent to the graph of $f$ at point $P.$

b. Determine the unit vector $\textbf{u}$ with initial point $P$ in the direction of vector $PQ.$

Consider $f$ and $g$ two functions defined on the same set of real numbers $D.$ Let $\text{a}=\langle x,f(x)\rangle$ and $\text{b}=\langle x,g(x)\rangle$ be two vectors that describe the graphs of the functions, where $x\in D.$ Show that if the graphs of the functions $f$ and $g$ do not intersect, then the vectors $\textbf{a}$ and $\textbf{b}$ are not equivalent.

answer.solution: Two vectors written in component form are equivalent exactly when their components are equal. Here $\mathbf{a}=\langle x,f(x)\rangle$ and $\mathbf{b}=\langle x,g(x)\rangle$ have the same first component, so they would be equivalent only if $f(x)=g(x).$ If the graphs of $f$ and $g$ do not intersect, there is no $x$ in $D$ with $f(x)=g(x),$ so the second components always differ, and for every $x$ in $D$ the vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ are not equivalent.

A bullet is fired with an initial velocity of $1500$ ft/sec at an angle of $60^{\circ}$ with the horizontal. Find the horizontal and vertical components of the velocity vector of the bullet. (Round to two decimal places.)

answer.solution: The horizontal and vertical components are $750$ ft/sec and $1299.04$ ft/sec, respectively.

answer.solution: The magnitude of resultant force is $94.71$ lb; the direction angle is $13.42^{\circ}.$

A guy-wire supports a pole that is $75$ ft high. One end of the wire is attached to the top of the pole and the other end is anchored to the ground $50$ ft from the base of the pole. Determine the horizontal and vertical components of the force of tension in the wire if its magnitude is $50$ lb. (Round to the nearest integer.)

answer.solution: The two horizontal and vertical components of the force of tension are $28$ lb and $42$ lb, respectively.
